The Aim

The common objective in empirical sciences is to learn something about a population

For example

  • What is the average annual salary among all working-age individuals in the UK
  • What is the average height among all students at the University of Glasgow
  • What is the average relationship between education and wages among all working-age individuals in the USA

Challenge: We rarely observe the full population.

However, we can use samples and tools of Econometrics and Statistics to learn something about the population

Data

Source: Current Population Survey (CPS)

  • Sample of 30,967 men living in the USA and born 1944–53
  • Years 1979 and 1981–85
  • Information about
    • Annual wage
    • Years of Education
    • Employment status
    • Age
  • The data are a repeated cross-section: a snapshot of potentially different individuals living in the USA at different points in time

Back to our Aim: Mathematical Expectation

Remember: we want to learn something about a population

One target: Mathematical Expectation (expected value) of outcome $Y_{i}$, $\EX[Y_{i}]$

  • Equivalent to the population mean or sample average in an infinite population

Examples:

  • Average annual salary among all individuals in the UK
  • Average height among all students at the University of Glasgow

Back to our Aim: Conditional Mathematical Expectation

Another target: Conditional Mathematical Expectation $\EX[Y_{i}\mid X_{i} = x]$

  • The conditional expectation of $Y_{i}$ given $X_{i}=x$ is the average of $Y_{i}$ in an infinite population when $X_{i}=x$

Example: Let $Y_{i}$ be a salary, and let $X_{i} \in \{0,1\}$ be a “Finnish football player indicator”

  • $\EX[Y_{i}\mid X_{i} = 1]$ is average salary among infinitely many Finnish football players
  • $\EX[Y_{i}\mid X_{i} = 0]$ is average salary among everybody else

Law of Large Numbers (LLN)

The Challenge: we want to learn something about a population but only observe a sample.

Solution: The Law of Large Numbers (LLN)

Sample moments converge in probability to the corresponding population moments. In other words, the probability that the sample mean is close to the population mean can be made as high as you like by taking a large enough sample.
Live demo: watch $\bar{Y}$ settle on $\EX[Y_i]$

Law of Large Numbers (LLN)

Basic idea: Suppose you have a randomly drawn sample from a population

  • In small samples, the realized average of $Y_{i}$ might be far from $\EX[Y_{i}]$
  • LLN says: Average of $Y_{i}$ ($\bar{Y}$) gets very close to $\EX[Y_{i}]$ as the number of observations ($n$) gets large \[ \bar{Y} \rightarrow \EX[Y_{i}] \quad \text{when} \quad n \rightarrow \infty \]

The sample average $\bar{Y}$ is an unbiased estimate of $\EX[Y_{i}]$ in any sample size, and by the LLN it is also consistent: as $n$ grows, $\bar{Y}$ gets arbitrarily close to $\EX[Y_{i}]$ $\rightarrow$ when $n$ is large enough, we can use $\bar{Y}$ to approximate $\EX[Y_{i}]$

Part 2

Ordinary Least Squares

Bivariate Analysis

  • So far, we have been mainly thinking about how to summarize information in one variable
  • What if we are interested in how two variables are related?
  • For example, what is the relationship between education and earnings?
  • We could use conditional expectations:
  • Suppose $Y_{i}$ is a salary, and let $X_{i} \in \{0,1\}$ be an indicator for having a university degree
  • Average difference in salary between high- and low-educated individuals would be \[ \EX[Y_{i}\mid X_{i} = 1] - \EX[Y_{i}\mid X_{i} = 0] \]
  • But what if $X_{i}$ is a continuous variable?

What is a linear regression?

  • A tool to describe the relationship between two variables in the data, e.g. earnings $Y_i$ and years of education $X_i$
  • In the simplest case, a straight line: the line that best describes how the average of $Y_i$ changes with $X_i$ (the conditional expectation). Ordinary least squares (OLS) is the algorithm that finds it
  • We can use the line to make predictions. Sometimes these predictions are causal, and sometimes not. This course is about telling the two apart

Years of Education and Earnings in CPS Data

  • Earnings vary a lot at every level of education
    • Other factors matter
    • Randomness
  • Still, a clear positive relationship
  • How can we summarize it?

A simple way to summarize the relationship between the two variables is to fit a line

We can write the functional form of this line as

\[ \text{earnings} = \alpha + \beta \times \text{education} \]
  • This is just the functional form of a straight line with two parameters:
    1. The intercept $(\alpha)$ tells us where the line crosses the y-axis
    2. The slope $(\beta)$ of the line tells us how much the earnings change if we increase the years of education by one

The Line

  • We want to find a line to be “as close as possible” to all the points in the data
  • How do we find this line? We use OLS. It finds parameters that make the fitted line “as close as possible” to the data
  • Specifically: OLS minimizes the sum of the squared deviations of the data from the regression line
  • Various statistical software packages will do this for you
Live demo: can you beat OLS by hand?

OLS

We can summarize the linear relationship between earnings and years of education with the simple linear OLS regression model:

\[ \text{earnings}_i = \alpha + \beta \times \text{education}_i + e_i \]
  • $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the regression coefficients that OLS finds; the subscript $i$ denotes individuals
  • $e_i$ is the error term: all the other factors influencing earnings besides years of education
  • Once OLS has fitted the line, the residual $\hat{e}_i$ is how far each individual's actual earnings are from the fitted line. It is our estimate of the unobserved error term $e_i$
LIVE DEMO
Find the best line: can you beat OLS by hand?
Try: Next step through 1–4: draw the data → fit a line → show the residuals → square them. Then drag the line to shrink the squares → Reveal the OLS line

What does the statistical software actually do?

  • When we run regressions, the statistical software solves the following problem
\[ \argmin_{\alpha,\beta}\; \EX\big[(Y_{i} - \alpha - \beta X_{i})^2\big] \]

The solution to this minimization problem happens to be

  • $\hat{\beta} = \dfrac{COV(Y_{i},X_{i})}{VAR(X_{i})}$
  • $\hat{\alpha} = \EX[Y_i] - \beta\, \EX[X_i]$
  • $\hat{\beta}$ and $\hat{\alpha}$ are called OLS estimators: they are simple algorithms applied to data

Three reasons to love OLS

Conditional expectation function (CEF): $\EX[Y_i \mid X_i = x]$, the average of $Y_i$ at each value of $X_i$

  1. OLS gives the best linear predictor of $Y_i$ given $X_i$
  2. If the CEF is linear, the regression line is the CEF
  3. If the CEF is not linear, regression gives the best linear approximation to the CEF

Take-away: regression is always a good summary of how the average of $Y_i$ changes with $X_i$. Whether that relationship is causal is a separate question, and that question is what this course is about.

Part 3

Statistical Inference

Sampling variation

  • Remember, we want to learn something about the population but we only observe a sample
  • Suppose we drew multiple random samples. With every draw, we would get a slightly different sample and estimates.
  • The estimates vary from sample to sample because of sampling variation
  • In other words, because the data are a random sample, our estimators are random variables
  • Sometimes, our estimate may be very extreme because we draw a very extreme sample
LIVE DEMO
Sampling variation: one sample, one slope
Try: Draw a new sample and run OLS, several times → change N to 30, then 1,000 → how much do the lines move?

The Central Limit Theorem Rescues Us

  • Fortunately, we can use statistics to infer whether our estimate carries a signal or is just noise
  • The most important building block is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT):
THE CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM Sample moments are asymptotically Normally distributed (after subtracting the corresponding population moment and multiplying by the square root of the sample size). In other words, in large enough samples, appropriately normalized sample moments are approximately Normally distributed.
  • CLT says that the distribution of sample means approximates a normal distribution as the sample size gets larger, regardless of the population's distribution.
LIVE DEMO
The central limit theorem
Try: n = 30: Draw 1 sample a few times, then 1,000 → try n = 1, 5, 30, 500 → tick the normal curve and zoom in → other populations

The Beauty of CLT

In a nutshell, the theorem says the following:

  1. We can start with any distribution of $Y_i$, possibly non-normal
  2. If we take the average of $Y_1,\dots,Y_N$ in a sample sufficiently large, the distribution of the sample average $\bar{Y}$ is (approximately) normal!

The Beauty of CLT

Central Limit theorem is the solution

In large samples, $\hat{\beta}$ is approximately normal:

\[ \hat{\beta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta, SE^2), \qquad SE = \frac{\bar{\sigma}}{\sqrt{N \times var(X)}} \]
  • Centred on the true $\beta$; its spread is the standard error
  • $\bar{\sigma}$ = SD of the residuals (Stata: “Root MSE”)
    • how far, typically, the observations are from the regression line
LIVE DEMO
The sampling distribution of β̂
Try: Draw 1,000 → tick Show the CLT curve (SD of the β̂'s vs the SE formula) → move one slider at a time: N, σ, SD of education

Central Limit theorem is the solution

What do we learn from this?

\[ \hat{\beta} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\beta, \frac{{\color{#c81e1e}\bar{\sigma}^2}}{{\color{#1d4ed8}N} \times {\color{#15803d}var(X)}}\right) \]
  • The larger the standard deviation of the residuals ${\color{#c81e1e}\bar{\sigma}}$, the more noise and the less signal there is in our estimate
  • The more observations ${\color{#1d4ed8}N}$ we have, the more precise the estimate
  • The more variation in $X$ (${\color{#15803d}var(X)}$), the more precise the estimate

Hypothesis Testing

  • We can use the property $\hat{\beta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta, SE^2)$ to test if our estimate is significant in a statistical sense
  • In hypothesis testing, we make two hypotheses
    1. Null hypothesis $H_0$
      • the version of the truth we're testing to see whether we can prove it's wrong
      • Often $H_0: \beta = 0$
    2. Alternative hypothesis $H_a$
      • Every version of the truth that's not the null hypothesis
      • Often $H_a: \beta \neq 0$

Hypothesis Testing

Now assume $H_0: \beta = 0$, $H_a: \beta \neq 0$

  • Under this null, we calculate the test statistic \[ \textit{t statistic} = \frac{\hat{\beta} - 0}{SE} = \frac{\hat{\beta}}{SE} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \]
  • The t statistic measures how extreme the observed difference is
  • We then ask: “Is such a t statistic likely if the null hypothesis is true?”
  • We answer this using the fact that the t statistic is standard normal

Example: Wages and Schooling

Live demo: from our t to a p-value

The Distribution of the test statistic if the null is true

Drag the red line to try another t  ·  back to t = 2.71
  • In our data we have one sample, so we observe one t statistic: $t = 2.71$
  • Is 2.71 large or small? On its own, we cannot tell
  • We need something to compare it to
  • Thought experiment: if $H_0$ were true and we could draw many repeated samples, computing $t$ in each, we would see this sampling distribution
  • In reality we have one sample, so we see only one $t$ (2.71), never this distribution. But the CLT tells us its shape: approximately standard normal, centred at 0
  • If $H_0$ is true, $t$ falls between $-1.96$ and $1.96$ 95% of the time
  • If $|t| > 1.96 \approx 2$, we reject $H_0$ at the 5% significance level
  • We then say the estimate is statistically significant
  • We can calculate the probability of seeing a $t$ at least as extreme as ours (in either direction), if $H_0$ is true: only 0.7%
  • This is the p-value: p = 0.007, so we reject H₀ even at the 1% level

Confidence intervals

We can also build confidence intervals

\[ \hat{\beta} \pm Z \times SE \]

Where $Z$ represents our confidence level, and SE stands for standard error

In the wages and schooling example, 95 percent confidence intervals are

\[ [\,0.046 - 1.96 \times 0.017\,,\; 0.046 + 1.96 \times 0.017\,] = [\,0.012\,,\; 0.079\,] \]

A confidence interval shows the range of nulls that our estimate would not reject.

Live demo: 100 studies, 100 intervals, one truth

Confidence intervals: the picture

  • 0 lies outside the interval $\Leftrightarrow$ we reject $H_0: \beta = 0$ at the 5% level (as $|t| = 2.71 > 1.96$)
  • Any value inside the interval, e.g. $\beta = 0.03$, would not be rejected: the interval is the set of null values consistent with our data

Appendix

Appendix: how is the p-value calculated?

Generic case. Let $T$ be the test statistic, with CDF $F(x) = P(T \leq x)$ if $H_0$ is true. Assume $T$ is continuous, and let $a = |t_{\text{obs}}|$ be the absolute value of our observed t statistic.

  1. Split the two tails: \[ p = P(|T| \geq a) = P(T \geq a) + P(T \leq -a) \]
  2. Write each tail with the CDF: \[ p = \big(1 - F(a)\big) + F(-a) \]

This holds for any continuous distribution.

Add symmetry. If the distribution is symmetric around 0, then $F(-a) = 1 - F(a)$, so

\[ p = 2\big(1 - F(a)\big) \]

Appendix: how is the p-value calculated?

Impose normality. If $H_0$ is true, $T \overset{a}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, so $F = \Phi$ (the standard normal CDF):

\[ p = 2\big(1 - \Phi(|t_{\text{obs}}|)\big) \]

Wages and schooling example: $t_{\text{obs}} = 2.71$

\[ p = 2\big(1 - \Phi(2.71)\big) = 2\,(1 - 0.9966) = 0.0067 \approx \textcolor{#c81e1e}{\mathbf{0.007}} \]

Exact t test. The same steps give the exact t-test p-value: set $F = F_{t_{n-k}}$, the CDF of the t distribution with $n - k$ degrees of freedom, which is also symmetric around 0.

  • This is what Stata reports in the P>|t| column: with $n - k = 163$, $p = 0.0075 \approx 0.007$
  • In large samples the two are almost identical, because $t_{n-k}$ approaches $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ as $n$ grows
